title: The Bridge That Learned to Dance
paragraphs: In 1940, a newly built suspension bridge began to move strangely whenever strong winds blew across the valley where it stood. Instead of remaining still like other bridges of its time, it swayed from side to side and, on particularly windy days, even twisted like a ribbon caught in the wind. At first, engineers assumed the movement was harmless and simply a curious feature of the design. However, the swinging grew worse over time, and just a few months after the bridge opened, it collapsed completely into the river below. Remarkably, no earthquake, accident, or structural defect in the materials caused the fall.

After the collapse, a team of engineers and physicists studied recordings of the bridge's movement and discovered that the wind had been creating a repeated force that matched the bridge's natural rhythm, in the same way that pushing a swing at just the right moment makes it go higher and higher. Once this rhythm was established, the bridge began to bend more and more with every gust until the material could no longer hold. Experts often compare this effect to the old military rule that soldiers must break step when crossing a bridge, since marching in unison can create the same kind of dangerous rhythm.

The collapse became one of the most studied events in the history of civil engineering. Films of the bridge swaying and finally falling are still shown in university courses today, since they illustrate the danger so clearly. As a direct result of the disaster, modern suspension bridges are now tested extensively in wind tunnels before construction, and many designs include dampers, devices built specifically to absorb this kind of repeated movement before it becomes dangerous.

title: The Customer Who Sued Over a Cup of Coffee
paragraphs: Years ago, a customer at a fast-food restaurant was sitting in a parked car when she opened a cup of coffee that had just been handed to her through the drive-through window. The cup slipped, and the coffee, which had been served at a temperature close to boiling, spilled across her lap. The burns she suffered were severe enough to require medical treatment and, according to court records, several skin grafts. She later sued the restaurant chain, arguing that serving coffee at such an extreme temperature made the product unreasonably dangerous for ordinary use.

Many people who first heard about the case found it hard to believe, assuming that coffee is simply supposed to be served hot and that the lawsuit was an example of someone blaming a company for their own accident. During the trial, however, evidence showed that the company had received hundreds of similar complaints about burns over the previous decade and had never changed its policy on serving temperature. Based on this evidence, the jury ultimately decided in favor of the customer, concluding that the company had been aware of the risk and had failed to act on it.

The case quickly became famous, and for years it was mentioned in the media as an example of an unnecessary lawsuit. More recently, however, legal experts and law schools have used it to teach a more careful lesson: it shows how a company's prior knowledge of a danger, combined with its decision to do nothing about it, can create genuine legal responsibility, regardless of how ordinary the product might seem.

title: The Shipping Box That Changed the World
paragraphs: Before the middle of the twentieth century, loading and unloading cargo ships was slow, expensive, and often dangerous work. Dockworkers carried goods off ships piece by piece, box by box, sack by sack, and a single medium-sized ship could take more than a week to load completely. Because so many hands touched every item along the way, theft was common, and shipping companies routinely built the cost of stolen goods into their prices.

Everything changed with a surprisingly simple idea: a steel box built in a standard size that could be lifted directly by a crane from the back of a truck onto a ship, without anyone needing to open it or touch what was inside. The idea is often credited to a truck driver who grew frustrated after spending hours waiting at a dock while his cargo was unloaded box by box. Shipping companies were initially skeptical that such a simple change could matter much, but early trials showed that a single container could be loaded in a fraction of the time it once took to move the same goods manually.

Within a few decades, this standardized container had reshaped global trade almost entirely. Ports could move far more cargo with far fewer workers, shipping costs dropped dramatically, and theft became far less common since goods were rarely handled individually. This made it cheaper to manufacture products in one country and sell them on the other side of the world, a pattern that defines much of today's global economy. Some historians argue that this simple steel box did more to globalize trade than any single international trade agreement.

title: When a Painting Ended Up in Court
paragraphs: A wealthy art collector once purchased a painting believed to be an original work by a famous artist, paying an enormous sum of money after the gallery assured him of its authenticity. For years, the painting held a prominent place in his private collection, admired by visitors and occasionally loaned to museums for special exhibitions.

Doubts began to surface when a group of independent experts was invited to examine the piece using modern chemical analysis. By studying the pigments used in the paint and the age of the canvas fibers, the experts concluded that the painting had almost certainly been created decades after the artist's death, meaning it could not possibly be an original. The collector, feeling deceived, sued the gallery that had sold him the piece, demanding a full refund plus damages for the emotional and financial loss.

The gallery, for its part, insisted that it had genuinely believed the painting was authentic at the time of the sale and had relied on the same experts who were considered reliable at the time. After reviewing the evidence, the court ruled that the gallery had not acted with any intent to deceive the buyer, but it still ordered a partial refund, since the painting's true value was far lower than what the collector had paid. The case became widely discussed in both legal and art circles, raising uncomfortable questions about exactly how confident experts must be before a piece of art can be confidently called genuine.

title: The Hospital That Talks by Text Message
paragraphs: In many rural areas, patients who needed medical attention, even for something as simple as a minor infection, often had to travel for hours to reach the nearest clinic or hospital. For elderly patients or families without reliable transportation, this meant that many health concerns were left untreated until they became more serious, simply because the trip itself was such a burden.

To address this problem, some clinics began offering medical consultations through text messages and video calls, allowing patients to describe their symptoms, share photographs when relevant, and receive medical guidance without leaving their homes. At first, a number of doctors were hesitant about this approach, worried that they might miss important physical signs, such as swelling, skin color, or breathing patterns, that are usually only noticeable during an in-person examination.

Over time, however, studies conducted at several clinics showed that this remote approach worked well for a wide range of common situations, including minor infections, questions about medication dosage, and routine follow-up appointments after minor surgery. For symptoms considered serious or unclear, doctors working online continue to direct patients to visit a hospital immediately rather than attempting to manage the situation remotely. This combination of remote guidance and in-person care, when necessary, has proven especially valuable for elderly patients and for anyone living far from a medical center.

title: The Four-Day Week Experiment
paragraphs: A mid-sized technology company decided to test a four-day work week without reducing employee salaries, largely out of curiosity about how the change might affect staff morale and long-term retention, not only productivity. During a six-month trial, employees across most departments worked one less day per week while keeping their full pay, and managers agreed to closely track output, sick leave, and general well-being throughout the experiment.

Contrary to what many managers expected, overall output did not drop. Employees reported feeling more focused during the hours they did work, took noticeably fewer sick days, and meetings became shorter overall, since staff were more conscious of protecting their now more limited working time. Internal surveys conducted before and after the trial showed that reported stress levels dropped by nearly a third, a result that surprised even the researchers hired to evaluate the experiment.

Not every department, however, experienced the same benefits. Customer service teams, which needed to remain available to clients throughout the entire week, found the new schedule considerably harder to manage, often requiring more complicated shift arrangements among fewer available staff. After reviewing all the results, the company decided to continue the four-day week permanently for most departments, while adjusting the model for roles that required daily coverage. The experiment was later cited by other companies considering similar changes.

title: The Ad That Backfired
paragraphs: A well-known drink brand once launched a television and social media advertising campaign intended to appear playful, hopeful, and lighthearted. The advertisement showed two groups of people from very different backgrounds coming together in the middle of a tense public demonstration, resolving their differences by sharing the company's product. The marketing team behind the campaign believed the message would be seen as optimistic and unifying, especially among younger audiences.

Instead of receiving praise, the advertisement was criticized almost immediately after it was released. Critics argued that the ad trivialized a serious and ongoing social movement by suggesting that a complicated, emotionally difficult issue could be resolved simply by sharing a drink. Many also felt that the company was using real social tension purely to sell its product, without showing any genuine understanding of the issue it was referencing. Within a single day, the criticism had spread widely across social media, generating far more attention than the company had expected or wanted.

Facing mounting pressure, the company withdrew the advertisement entirely and issued a public apology within twenty-four hours of the first wave of criticism. Marketing professionals have since used the case in university courses and corporate training sessions to illustrate the risks of using sensitive social topics for commercial purposes without a deep understanding of public sentiment. Although the company's quick response was later praised as an example of appropriate crisis management, the original misstep still caused significant reputational damage in the weeks that followed.

title: The Office With No Bosses
paragraphs: A mid-sized software company made the unusual decision to remove all traditional management titles, allowing employees to organize themselves into project teams and make most operational decisions collectively rather than through a hierarchy of managers. Instead of a manager assigning tasks from above, employees were free to choose which projects to join based on their own interests and skills, and important decisions, from budgets to new hires, were made through open group discussion rather than requiring approval from a single person.

Supporters of the system pointed to clear benefits during the first two years. Employees reported feeling a stronger sense of ownership over their work, since decisions genuinely reflected group input rather than a manager's individual preference, and several teams credited the system with encouraging more creative solutions than the company had previously produced under a traditional structure. Employee satisfaction surveys during this period also showed noticeably higher scores compared to the years before the change.

Over time, however, certain problems became harder to ignore. Without a single person responsible for making final calls, some decisions took far longer than they would have under traditional management, and disagreements between team members were more difficult to resolve since no one held clear authority to settle disputes. After several years of operating this way, the company adjusted its model, introducing a small number of coordinators whose main role was to help resolve conflicts and speed up decision-making, while the majority of day-to-day decisions remained shared among employees.

title: The Invisible Cost of Burnout
paragraphs: For many years, exhaustion caused by work was treated primarily as a personal problem, something individual employees were simply expected to manage on their own through rest, willpower, or, if necessary, quietly changing jobs. Employers rarely considered it something the organization itself was responsible for addressing, and workers who struggled were often quietly labeled as simply unable to handle pressure.

More recently, researchers and major health organizations have begun recognizing burnout as a legitimate occupational condition, closely linked to prolonged workplace stress that has not been successfully managed over time. Several long-term studies now suggest that burnout affects far more than a person's mood or motivation: it has been connected to ongoing sleep problems, a weakened immune system, and, in more severe and prolonged cases, an increased risk of heart-related health issues.

Companies that continue to ignore this shift in understanding often experience higher rates of employee turnover and noticeably lower overall productivity, even though these costs tend to be far less visible than something like a factory accident or a sudden financial loss on a balance sheet. Partly in response to this growing body of research, a number of organizations have begun offering dedicated mental health resources, actively adjusting unreasonable workloads, and training managers specifically to recognize the early warning signs of burnout well before it becomes severe enough to force an employee to leave entirely.

title: The Delivery Robot Problem
paragraphs: In several cities around the world, delivery companies began testing small robots designed to travel along public sidewalks, carrying packages directly to customers' doors without any human driver involved. The technology promised faster, cheaper deliveries and, in theory, fewer delivery vehicles clogging city streets during busy hours. Early trials were often celebrated by local media as an exciting glimpse of how urban delivery might work in the near future.

Reality, however, proved more complicated than expected. Pedestrians in several cities complained that the robots sometimes blocked narrow sidewalks entirely, forcing people to step into the street, or moved unpredictably around children, older adults, and people using wheelchairs. City officials, meanwhile, struggled to determine which existing traffic and safety laws even applied to these machines, since sidewalks had historically never been designed with any kind of vehicle, however small, in mind.

Different cities responded in very different ways. Some created entirely new rules, limiting how fast the robots could travel and requiring delivery companies to obtain special operating permits before deploying them on public sidewalks. Other cities, facing strong public pressure, chose to ban the robots altogether until clearer, more complete regulations could be developed and properly tested. Many observers have pointed to this situation as a clear example of a common pattern in modern technology: innovation frequently moves far faster than the legal and regulatory systems originally designed to manage it.

title: The Paradox of Choice in the Modern Supermarket
paragraphs: Modern supermarkets take pride in offering extraordinary variety: entire aisles devoted to nothing but salad dressing, dozens of near-identical yogurt brands, and shelves of cereal boxes that seem to multiply every year. Conventional wisdom holds that more options should make consumers happier, since a wider selection presumably increases the odds that shoppers will find exactly what they want. Yet a growing body of research in behavioral economics suggests the opposite may often be true.

In a now well-known series of experiments, researchers set up sampling tables offering shoppers either a small selection of six jams or an extensive display of twenty-four. Counterintuitively, the smaller display attracted fewer initial visitors but generated substantially more purchases, while the larger display drew more curious browsers who ultimately walked away empty-handed. The explanation researchers proposed is not that people dislike variety itself, but that an overwhelming number of options increases what psychologists call cognitive load, the mental effort required to compare and evaluate alternatives. Beyond a certain threshold, this effort becomes so taxing that many consumers simply postpone the decision altogether rather than risk choosing incorrectly.

This phenomenon, sometimes labeled the paradox of choice, carries implications well beyond grocery aisles. Some retailers have begun deliberately trimming their product lines, wagering that a curated selection will boost both sales and customer satisfaction, even at the cost of appearing less comprehensive. Critics of this approach, however, argue that reducing choice can also be paternalistic, effectively deciding for consumers what they should want rather than trusting them to navigate abundance on their own. Whether excessive choice is a genuine psychological burden or merely an inconvenience easily solved by better store design remains a matter of ongoing debate among researchers.

title: When Algorithms Decide Who Gets the Loan
paragraphs: Banks have increasingly turned to automated systems to determine who qualifies for a loan, arguing that algorithms can evaluate applications more quickly and, in theory, more objectively than a human loan officer influenced by personal bias. These systems typically analyze thousands of data points, from credit history to spending patterns, to calculate a risk score that determines approval.

Proponents of this shift emphasize efficiency and consistency: a well-designed algorithm applies the same criteria to every applicant, removing the possibility that a loan officer might unconsciously favor certain applicants over others. However, a growing number of studies have identified a troubling irony. Because these systems are trained on historical lending data, they can inadvertently learn and perpetuate the very biases they were meant to eliminate. If a bank historically approved fewer loans for applicants from a particular neighborhood, an algorithm trained on that data may continue rejecting similar applicants today, even if it never explicitly considers their location as a factor, since other variables in the data may serve as unintentional proxies for it.

Regulators have struggled to address this problem, partly because many lending algorithms function as so-called black boxes: their internal decision-making processes are so complex that even the engineers who built them cannot always explain exactly why a specific application was rejected. Some financial institutions now employ specialists whose sole responsibility is to audit these systems for hidden discriminatory patterns, though critics argue this oversight often occurs only after damage has already been done to the applicants involved. The debate ultimately raises a difficult question: can a system be considered fair simply because it avoids human prejudice, if it merely reproduces that same prejudice through different, less visible means?

title: The Silent Epidemic: Antibiotic Resistance Explained
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, antibiotics transformed medicine, turning once-fatal bacterial infections into minor, easily treated conditions. Today, however, public health officials warn of a quieter but equally serious threat: bacteria that no longer respond to the drugs designed to kill them.

Antibiotic resistance develops through natural evolutionary pressure. Whenever antibiotics are used, most bacteria die, but a small number carrying random genetic mutations may survive by chance. These survivors reproduce, gradually passing on their resistance to future generations. The more frequently antibiotics are used, particularly when prescribed unnecessarily for viral illnesses they cannot treat, or when patients fail to complete a full prescribed course, the faster this evolutionary process accelerates, effectively training bacteria to withstand treatment.

The consequences extend far beyond individual patients. Hospitals increasingly report infections that respond to few, if any, available antibiotics, forcing doctors to rely on older, more toxic drugs, or, in the most severe cases, leaving few treatment options at all. Some researchers describe this trend as a slow-motion crisis, one that lacks the dramatic, sudden visibility of an outbreak but may ultimately prove more difficult to reverse, since developing new antibiotics has become commercially unattractive for pharmaceutical companies, who often earn far more from long-term treatments for chronic conditions than from short courses of antibiotics meant to cure an infection quickly.

title: Who Owns an Idea? The Strange History of Patent Disputes
paragraphs: Patent law exists, in theory, to strike a careful balance: rewarding inventors for their creativity by granting them temporary exclusive rights, while ultimately ensuring that useful knowledge eventually enters the public domain for society's broader benefit. In practice, however, the history of patent disputes reveals just how difficult this balance can be to maintain.

Consider the case of two inventors who, working independently and without any apparent contact, filed remarkably similar patents for the same basic technology within weeks of each other. Deciding who deserves credit, and the accompanying financial rewards, in such situations has proven notoriously difficult, since simultaneous discovery is far more common in the history of innovation than most people assume; ideas frequently emerge from shared scientific or technological conditions rather than from a single moment of individual genius, however appealing that narrative may be.

Modern patent disputes have grown considerably more complicated still, particularly in industries built on incremental innovation, where thousands of small, overlapping patents can apply to a single product. Critics argue that this fragmentation, sometimes described as a patent thicket, discourages genuine innovation rather than protecting it, since companies must navigate a dense web of potential lawsuits before releasing anything new, arguably diverting resources away from research and toward litigation. Defenders of the current system counter that without strong patent protections, companies would have little incentive to invest in expensive, uncertain research in the first place, since competitors could simply copy any successful innovation without bearing any of the original development costs.

Neither position has definitively prevailed, and the tension between rewarding individual invention and preserving the free flow of ideas remains, arguably, one of the more persistent unresolved questions in innovation policy.

title: The Engineer Who Said No
paragraphs: In the lead-up to a scheduled product launch, an engineer at a manufacturing company discovered a flaw in a critical safety component during a routine final inspection. The defect was subtle, unlikely to cause failure under normal conditions, but capable, under a specific and admittedly rare combination of circumstances, of producing a serious malfunction. Delaying the launch to address the problem would have meant missing a contractual deadline, incurring significant financial penalties, and disappointing a client the company had spent months courting.

Under considerable pressure from senior management, who argued that the probability of the flaw actually causing harm was statistically negligible, the engineer refused to approve the product for release. She insisted that any known safety risk, however small, needed to be addressed before shipment, regardless of the financial consequences the delay would create. Her decision was initially unpopular internally, and she reportedly faced significant tension with colleagues who felt she was being unnecessarily rigid about a theoretical risk.

Months later, a similar flaw in a competitor's product led to a widely publicized failure, causing considerable reputational and financial damage to that company. In light of this event, the engineer's earlier decision was publicly praised as an example of principled professional judgment, and her case has since been used in engineering ethics courses to illustrate the tension between commercial pressure and professional responsibility.

The case raises a broader question that extends well beyond this single incident: how should organizations weigh statistically small risks against significant, guaranteed costs, particularly when the person best equipped to assess the technical danger is not necessarily the person authorized to make the final commercial decision?

title: The Hidden Bias in Hiring Algorithms
paragraphs: As companies face growing volumes of job applications, many have turned to automated screening software to filter candidates before a human recruiter ever reviews a resume. These systems promise efficiency, and proponents argue they can reduce the unconscious bias that might otherwise influence a tired or overworked human reviewer scanning hundreds of applications.

However, several widely reported cases have revealed a troubling pattern: hiring algorithms trained on a company's historical hiring data can inherit and amplify existing biases embedded in that very data. In one notable example, a recruitment tool was found to systematically downgrade resumes containing words more commonly associated with women's professional and extracurricular activities, apparently because the historical data it had learned from reflected a workforce that had, for years, been predominantly male. The algorithm had not been explicitly programmed to discriminate; it had simply identified patterns in past hiring decisions and replicated them with mechanical consistency.

This phenomenon complicates the common assumption that removing a human decision-maker automatically produces a fairer outcome. Rather than eliminating bias, poorly audited algorithms risk encoding it more deeply and applying it at a much larger scale than any single human recruiter ever could. Some technology companies have responded by implementing regular bias audits and adjusting training data to correct known imbalances, while others have faced criticism for continuing to use systems whose decision-making processes remain largely opaque even to their own developers.

The broader lesson extends beyond hiring: whenever an algorithm learns from historical human decisions, it risks inheriting not only useful patterns but also the very prejudices those decisions once reflected.

title: The Economics of Attention
paragraphs: Nearly every major digital platform, from social media applications to streaming services, competes in what industry analysts increasingly describe as an attention economy, a marketplace in which the scarce resource being bought and sold is not information itself but the limited time and focus of human users. Since advertising revenue typically scales with the amount of time users spend engaged with a platform, companies have strong financial incentives to design products that maximize this engagement, sometimes regardless of whether that time genuinely benefits the user.

This incentive has shaped design choices in ways many users barely notice. Features such as infinite scrolling, which removes natural stopping points that might otherwise prompt a user to pause and reconsider, or variable reward systems, which mimic the unpredictable reinforcement patterns found in gambling, are not accidental; they emerge from careful experimentation aimed explicitly at maximizing the time users spend within an application. Some former designers of these very systems have since spoken publicly about their unease, describing a growing tension between what keeps users most engaged and what genuinely serves their broader well-being.

Critics argue that this model effectively treats human attention as an extractable resource, prioritizing short-term engagement metrics over any deeper concern for how users actually feel after using these products. Defenders of the industry counter that users retain agency and can simply choose to disengage at any time, and that blaming design alone risks ignoring individual responsibility entirely. Whether meaningful reform will come through voluntary industry change, government regulation, or simply a gradual shift in public awareness remains, for now, an open and contested question.

title: When the Sea Takes the Land Back
paragraphs: As sea levels gradually rise due to climate change, coastal communities around the world face a legal and philosophical question few property laws were ever designed to answer: what happens to ownership when the land itself physically disappears? In several coastal regions, property once clearly above the high-tide line has gradually become submerged, sometimes permanently, raising disputes over whether owners retain any rights to land that technically no longer exists in any usable form.

Traditional property law generally assumes that land boundaries are fixed and stable, changing only through deliberate human action such as a sale or a legal transfer. Gradual environmental change was rarely anticipated as a mechanism through which ownership itself might dissolve. In some jurisdictions, courts have ruled that once land is permanently submerged, ownership effectively lapses, leaving affected property owners with no compensation and no clear legal recourse, since no single identifiable party can be held directly responsible for a slow, global environmental process.

This has led some legal scholars to argue for entirely new frameworks, including collective compensation funds financed by industries most closely associated with greenhouse gas emissions, or updated property definitions that account explicitly for gradual environmental loss rather than treating it as legally invisible. Government officials, meanwhile, face immense practical and financial challenges in relocating entire communities, particularly when the economic and cultural cost of abandoning ancestral land is difficult to measure in purely monetary terms. As rising seas continue to reshape coastlines in the coming decades, courts and legislators alike will likely be forced to confront a question property law has, until recently, been able to comfortably avoid.

title: The Myth of Multitasking
paragraphs: Modern professional culture often celebrates the ability to multitask, treating the simultaneous handling of emails, phone calls, and reports as a mark of efficiency and even a competitive workplace advantage. Cognitive science, however, tells a considerably less flattering story about what actually happens in the brain when we attempt to juggle multiple demanding tasks at once.

Research consistently suggests that what people commonly call multitasking is, in most cases, actually rapid task-switching: the brain is not truly processing two complex tasks simultaneously but instead shifting attention back and forth between them at high speed. Each switch, however brief and seemingly effortless, carries a measurable cognitive cost, sometimes referred to as switching cost, which manifests as slower performance, more frequent errors, and, over time, noticeably increased mental fatigue. Studies estimate that heavy, habitual multitasking during complex cognitive work can reduce overall productivity substantially compared to focusing on a single task through to completion.

Interestingly, some people who multitask frequently believe themselves to be particularly skilled at it, a belief that research has repeatedly failed to support; if anything, several studies suggest that habitual multitaskers tend to perform somewhat worse on tests specifically designed to measure task-switching ability than people who multitask only occasionally. This apparent contradiction may stem from the fact that multitasking, while genuinely less efficient overall, can nonetheless feel more stimulating and engaging in the moment, creating a persistent but ultimately misleading impression of productivity.

Despite this substantial body of evidence, workplace norms have been remarkably slow to change, and many organizations continue, whether explicitly or implicitly, to reward employees who appear constantly available and responsive across multiple channels simultaneously, arguably reinforcing precisely the habits that cognitive research suggests undermine genuine productivity.

title: The Container Ship Stuck in the Canal
paragraphs: In 2021, a single massive container ship ran aground in a narrow but critically important shipping canal, wedging itself diagonally across the waterway and blocking all traffic in both directions for nearly a week. The incident, caused by a combination of high winds and, according to some investigators, navigational error, brought a striking illustration of just how concentrated and fragile global shipping infrastructure had become.

Although the canal represents only a small percentage of the earth's total ocean surface, it serves as a critical passage connecting major shipping routes, and an estimated significant share of global trade by volume passes through it annually. With hundreds of vessels unable to pass, some companies faced the difficult choice of waiting indefinitely or rerouting entirely around a different continent, adding weeks to delivery times and substantial fuel costs. Economists later estimated that the blockage delayed billions of dollars worth of goods, disrupting supply chains for industries ranging from retail to automotive manufacturing, many of which were already strained by other global disruptions at the time.

The event reignited a long-standing debate among logistics experts about the risks of an increasingly concentrated global supply chain, one built for efficiency and low cost rather than resilience against unexpected disruption. Some analysts have since argued for greater diversification of shipping routes and increased regional manufacturing, even at higher cost, to reduce dependence on any single vulnerable chokepoint. Others contend that such incidents, while dramatic, remain statistically rare, and that the economic benefits of the current highly efficient system still outweigh the costs of a more redundant, and considerably more expensive, alternative.
